paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately finite-rank kernel ridge regression predicts on unseen data. Existing guarantees for more general kernel regression can give overly loose bounds in this setting. That leaves a gap between having a theoretical guarantee and having one that usefully describes the particular model being trained.

The authors address this gap by deriving both upper and lower bounds on test error specifically for finite-rank kernel ridge regression. Together, these bounds constrain the error from both directions. The results are non-asymptotic, meaning they apply at finite sample sizes rather than only describing behavior as the amount of training data grows indefinitely.

The stated bounds improve on earlier finite-rank results and remain valid for any regularization parameter. This matters because the analysis continues to apply across choices of regularization strength. The setting also connects to transfer learning: adapting the last layer of a pretrained neural network is one situation where finite-rank kernels naturally arise. The contribution is therefore a sharper account of prediction error for a model class with practical relevance.
neurips-2023-a-theoretical-analysis-of-t.tldr: The paper derives tighter finite-sample bounds on finite-rank kernel ridge regression test error that remain valid across all regularization parameters.

paragraphs: This paper investigates adversarial vulnerability in two-layer ReLU networks under a specific geometric assumption: the training data lie within a low-dimensional linear subspace. This setting lets the authors distinguish changes that stay within the space occupied by the data from changes that move away from it.

The authors show that standard gradient training methods produce networks with large gradients in directions orthogonal to the data subspace. A large gradient means that a small movement in such a direction can substantially change the network's output. They connect this behavior to susceptibility to adversarial perturbations that are small in Euclidean, or L2, distance.

The analysis also identifies two ways to improve robustness in these orthogonal directions: reducing the scale of the initial parameters or adding L2 regularization during training. These results connect vulnerability to choices made by the training algorithm. Their scope is the stated network and data setting, with robustness improvements specifically concerning perturbations orthogonal to the data; they do not establish universal protection against adversarial changes.
neurips-2023-adversarial-examples-exist-.tldr: For two-layer ReLU networks trained on a low-dimensional linear subspace, the paper explains vulnerability to orthogonal perturbations and identifies training choices that can improve robustness.

paragraphs: Robust learning often depends on knowing which changes an adversary is allowed to make to an input. In practice, a learner may have some information about these changes without knowing their exact boundaries. This paper studies that middle position by giving the learner a class of possible perturbation sets.

The authors show that this partial knowledge can improve learnability results compared with a setting where perturbation sets are completely unknown. In particular, they obtain positive results for infinite Littlestone classes when a perfect-attack oracle is available. The oracle assumption is part of the result: the learner has access to an idealized mechanism for identifying attacks.

The paper also studies learners that can abstain from predicting. In this formulation, a robustness violation occurs when the learner makes an incorrect prediction within the perturbation set. The authors identify classes where learning without knowledge of that set and without query access is possible, but requires abstention. The findings show that both partial information about attacks and the option to withhold a prediction can change what robust learning can achieve.
neurips-2023-adversarially-robust-learni.tldr: Partial knowledge of possible adversarial perturbations and the option to abstain enable robust learnability results under the paper's stated information assumptions.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a decision-making policy from an existing dataset without collecting new experience. A common safeguard keeps the learned policy close to behaviors represented in that data. However, when most recorded trajectories come from weak policies, this safeguard can also encourage imitation of the behaviors that dominate the dataset.

The paper proposes changing which parts of the dataset guide that constraint. Instead of treating the entire collection as the desired reference, the method aims to align learning with the policy responsible for its good portions. It optimizes importance sampling weights to emulate drawing data from a distribution produced by a nearly optimal policy.

This makes the relative influence of recorded experience central to handling imbalance. The authors evaluate the approach with leading offline reinforcement learning algorithms across 72 datasets containing different types of imbalance. They report substantial gains over existing approaches, reaching up to fivefold improvement. That figure describes the largest reported gain, rather than an improvement established for every dataset or every offline learning problem.
neurips-2023-beyond-uniform-sampling-off.tldr: Optimizing sampling weights toward better recorded behavior improves offline reinforcement learning on imbalanced datasets, with reported gains of up to fivefold.

paragraphs: CELL-E 2 connects two ways of describing a protein: its amino acid sequence and images showing where it localizes inside a cell. The paper treats localization as a problem requiring both sequence information and spatial information. Its transformer works in both directions, generating localization images from sequences and generating sequences from images.

Building on CELL-E, the model represents the spatial complexity of localization and produces probability estimates over a nucleus image. This gives the sequence-to-image direction a spatial output, showing how localization is distributed in the image. The reverse direction supports de novo protein design by allowing image information to guide the generation of new sequences.

The authors train and fine-tune the model using two large datasets of human proteins. They also demonstrate a use case that creates hundreds of novel nuclear localization signals. This application illustrates how a bidirectional model can connect localization prediction with sequence generation. The stated contribution is the ability to move between these representations and use that connection for design; the abstract does not claim experimental biological validation of every generated signal.
neurips-2023-celle-2-translating-protein.tldr: CELL-E 2 translates between protein sequences and localization images, supporting spatial prediction and generation of new protein sequences.

paragraphs: Cooperative communication depends on common ground: enough shared knowledge for one participant to understand another. The paper argues that earlier models assume perfect and complete knowledge sharing, removing a central difficulty of communication from the model itself. It develops a theory that allows different degrees of shared understanding.

The framework explicitly describes a spectrum of common-ground possibilities and accommodates arbitrary representations of data and hypotheses. It strictly generalizes prior cooperative communication models, so those earlier models remain covered within a broader mathematical account. This makes incomplete sharing something the theory can represent directly rather than something excluded by its starting assumptions.

The authors then consider a parameterized form of common ground. They interpret choosing communicative data as encoding and inferring a hypothesis from that data as decoding. Through this formulation, they establish a connection to variational autoencoding. Empirical simulations support and elaborate on the theoretical results. The contribution links a more flexible theory of shared understanding with a machine-learning framework for encoding and decoding information.
neurips-2023-common-ground-in-cooperativ.tldr: The paper generalizes cooperative communication models to incomplete common ground and connects a parameterized formulation to variational autoencoding.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes direct policy search for structured H-infinity control with static output feedback. Structural constraints make the optimization problem constrained, nonconvex, and nonsmooth. The authors ask how much computation or trajectory data is needed when the optimizer can evaluate control performance but cannot access its derivatives.

They first study an exact oracle that returns the closed-loop system's H-infinity norm. Using a property of the cost function called coerciveness, they establish high-probability bounds on feasibility and optimization complexity. The target is a specified form of approximate stationarity, expressed through delta and epsilon, rather than a guarantee of finding the globally best controller.

The authors next derive a sample complexity result for estimating the H-infinity norm of systems with multiple inputs and outputs. Combining this estimator with the optimization analysis yields their stated first sample complexity guarantee for model-free, trajectory-based, zeroth-order optimization in this structured control setting. Numerical results illustrate the theory. The combined analysis connects idealized access to exact performance values with the more practical task of estimating those values from system trajectories.
neurips-2023-complexity-of-derivative-fr.tldr: The paper gives complexity guarantees for derivative-free structured H-infinity control, including a trajectory-based route to approximate stationary points.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries by exploiting a simple underlying structure, such as low rank. Producing an estimate is only part of the problem: users also need a meaningful indication of its uncertainty. The paper addresses the sensitivity of existing uncertainty methods to an incorrect structural model.

The proposed method, conformalized matrix completion, adapts conformal prediction from regression to missing matrix entries. Its purpose is to produce prediction intervals with provable coverage. Crucially, the stated coverage guarantee does not depend on the low-rank model being accurate, separating the reliability of predictive coverage from the correctness of that model.

Experiments on simulated and real data show robustness when the assumed model is misspecified. When the model is correct, the method matches the performance of existing model-based approaches. These findings suggest that robustness to structural mistakes need not come at the expense of performance in the correctly specified cases examined. The paper's central contribution is a distribution-free approach to predictive inference for matrix completion, extending the task beyond filling in a single value.
neurips-2023-conformalized-matrix-comple.tldr: Conformalized matrix completion provides prediction intervals with provable coverage regardless of the low-rank model's accuracy.

paragraphs: Continuously publishing the number of distinct items becomes harder when a data stream allows deletions as well as insertions. The paper proves that every differentially private mechanism for this setting must incur worst-case additive error of at least T to the one-quarter power, where T is stream length. This holds even under event-level privacy and without memory restrictions.

The authors then identify a property that makes some streams easier: maximum flippancy. It counts the largest number of times any individual item's contribution to the distinct count changes. Their item-level private mechanism adapts without knowing this quantity in advance, achieving error proportional to its square root times a polylogarithmic factor in stream length.

For a large range of flippancy values, the authors establish that their dependence on this parameter is the best achievable for bounds depending only on it. When flippancy is small, the error resembles that of insertion-only streams. The result therefore distinguishes worst-case difficulty from achievable accuracy on streams where individual items change their counted status relatively infrequently.
neurips-2023-counting-distinct-elements-.tldr: Private distinct counting with deletions has substantial worst-case error, but an adaptive mechanism achieves much better accuracy when items rarely change their counted status.

paragraphs: Nanophotonic design seeks structures with useful optical properties for applications such as solar cells, coatings, filters, and light-emitting diodes. Evaluating a candidate requires electrodynamic simulation, which models electromagnetic fields over time and calculates the resulting optical behavior. These evaluations are central to deciding whether a proposed design meets its target.

The paper introduces frameworks and benchmarks for design problems expressed through structural parameters. They provide a setting in which optimization algorithms can be assessed according to their ability to identify structures with desired optical properties. This connects algorithm evaluation to the actual design objective: finding a suitable physical structure through simulation.

The authors also investigate how changing the simulation grid size affects evaluation fidelity. This brings the resolution of the evaluation itself into the design problem, alongside the parameters of the structure being optimized. Their exploration examines how fidelity can be used strategically to improve designs. The contribution combines benchmarks for comparing optimization methods with an investigation of how the simulation choices supporting those comparisons influence the design process.
neurips-2023-datasets-and-benchmarks-for.tldr: The paper introduces nanophotonic design benchmarks and investigates how simulation grid size and evaluation fidelity can support better structure optimization.

paragraphs: Transferring step-by-step language reasoning to tasks involving images introduces challenges in annotation effort, flexibility, generalization, and explanation. This paper examines those challenges and proposes DDCoT, a prompting method organized around two ideas: maintaining a critical attitude during reasoning and assigning different responsibilities to language and visual models.

DDCoT separates reasoning from recognition. It incorporates visual models' recognition capabilities into a joint reasoning process, while using negative-space prompting to encourage a critical stance. This division makes visual recognition an explicit component of how the answer is developed, with the language model's reasoning responsibility distinguished from the task of interpreting visual content.

The generated rationales are used in both zero-shot prompting and fine-tuning. The authors report that they improve reasoning for both large and small language models and significantly outperform state-of-the-art methods in their evaluation. They also report strong generalizability and explainability. The contribution is a method for coordinating multimodal reasoning responsibilities, with empirical evidence that the resulting explanations can help models across different sizes and learning settings.
neurips-2023-ddcot-duty-distinct-chain-o.tldr: DDCoT coordinates language reasoning and visual recognition to generate rationales that improve multimodal performance in prompting and fine-tuning experiments.

paragraphs: A Gaussian mixture of experts combines expert predictions using a softmax gate. This paper studies how accurately the model's parameters can be estimated, a theoretical problem complicated by the relationship between the gate and the experts. Understanding that relationship is necessary for describing how parameter estimates improve with more data.

The authors identify three obstacles. Parameters are identifiable only up to translation, so different parameter descriptions can be equivalent. The gating and expert functions also interact through partial differential equations, while the numerator and denominator of the conditional density have a complex dependence. These features make a straightforward treatment of parameter error inadequate.

To address these challenges, the paper introduces Voronoi loss functions for comparing parameters and establishes convergence rates for maximum likelihood estimation. When the fitted model contains more experts than the unknown true number, the authors connect those rates to whether a system of polynomial equations is solvable. This gives an algebraic characterization of an aspect of estimation difficulty, linking the behavior of an oversized mixture model to a concrete mathematical problem.
neurips-2023-demystifying-softmax-gating.tldr: New parameter loss functions establish maximum likelihood convergence rates for softmax-gated Gaussian experts, with over-specification linked to polynomial solvability.

paragraphs: Selecting a smaller training dataset can reduce learning costs, but model-specific selection methods often require the selection process to restart for each architecture. SubSelNet addresses this lack of reuse by building a framework that can select data across models without explicitly training every model to guide the selection.

Its central component is an attention-based predictor that uses the graph structure of a neural architecture. This component approximates the predictions of a trained network. Those approximate predictions then guide subset samplers, replacing an expensive source of information for data selection with a learned surrogate.

The framework has two variants with different requirements for a new model. Transductive SubSelNet solves a small optimization problem to choose its subset, using the surrogate to make that step fast. Inductive SubSelNet uses a trained selector and requires no selection-time optimization. Experiments across several real datasets show improvements over several existing methods. The contribution is therefore both a way to approximate model behavior for selection and two ways to turn that approximation into reusable data-selection machinery.
neurips-2023-efficient-data-subset-selec.tldr: SubSelNet uses architecture-based prediction surrogates to select training subsets across models through either lightweight optimization or a trained selector.

paragraphs: Fair principal component analysis seeks a representation whose projected distributions match across groups defined by sensitive attributes. This paper addresses two obstacles: the lack of a statistical learnability foundation for fair PCA and the memory demands of methods that require access to the entire dataset.

The authors introduce probably approximately fair and optimal learnability, abbreviated PAFO, to express the statistical objective. They then formulate a streaming version of fair PCA and propose the fair noisy power method. The streaming approach is designed to operate with limited memory, and the paper provides a PAFO-based statistical guarantee for the algorithm.

The practical evaluation uses CelebA without preprocessing. In the setting examined, existing approaches are inapplicable because of their memory requirements, while the streaming method performs fair PCA efficiently and effectively. The contribution joins a formal account of learning a fair representation with an algorithm suited to constrained memory. Its fairness goal concerns matching projected distributions conditional on sensitive attributes, which is the particular notion analyzed by the paper.
neurips-2023-fair-streaming-principal-co.tldr: The paper establishes a learnability framework for fair PCA and develops a memory-efficient streaming algorithm with a corresponding statistical guarantee.

paragraphs: HeadSculpt generates and edits three-dimensional head avatars from text. The paper targets two weaknesses of existing approaches: inconsistent or distorted geometry when relying on two-dimensional diffusion models, and limited control over detailed edits. Its coarse-to-fine pipeline adds information about head structure and viewing direction to address these problems.

For generation, the method combines landmark-based control with a learned textual embedding representing the appearance of the back of a head. These components give the diffusion model additional three-dimensional awareness and head-specific guidance. Their role is to support consistent avatar generation across views, addressing information that a general text-to-image model may not adequately provide.

For editing, HeadSculpt introduces identity-aware score distillation and optimizes a textured mesh using high-resolution differentiable rendering. The editing strategy aims to follow the requested change while preserving the avatar's identity. Experiments and comparisons with existing methods demonstrate superior fidelity and editing capabilities in the reported evaluation. The contribution combines guidance for consistent head generation with an editing objective that explicitly accounts for identity preservation.
neurips-2023-headsculpt-crafting-3d-head.tldr: HeadSculpt combines head-specific 3D guidance and identity-aware mesh editing to generate and modify head avatars from text.

paragraphs: A model can make systematic mistakes on a subset of examples that share recognizable attributes. Finding these subsets and explaining what they have in common is useful for debugging, but existing approaches can demand extensive human inspection and annotation. HiBug aims to automate this process while keeping its findings understandable.

The framework uses large pretrained models, including ChatGPT, to suggest attributes relevant to a computer vision task. Pretrained vision-language models then help identify shared visual attributes in underperforming data slices. This links failures to descriptions that people can interpret, turning a collection of errors into a more specific account of where the model struggles.

The authors describe using these findings to uncover rare training cases and identify spurious correlations in the model. The explanations can also guide the selection or generation of additional training data for improvement. Experimental results support the framework's efficacy. HiBug's contribution is therefore a connection between automated error discovery, interpretable descriptions of failing subsets, and data choices informed by those descriptions.
neurips-2023-hibug-on-human-interpretabl.tldr: HiBug uses pretrained language and vision-language models to explain underperforming data slices and guide the collection or generation of corrective training data.

paragraphs: In reinforcement learning, an agent may struggle to discover useful behavior when rewards are sparse. Demonstrations can guide exploration, but high-quality examples may be expensive or unavailable. HYPO addresses this situation by using a small number of imperfect demonstrations to accelerate learning through subsequent interaction with the environment.

The method first uses imitation learning to train an offline guider policy. That guider helps an online agent policy explore more efficiently. The two policies then undergo mutual updates, allowing the agent to benefit from suboptimal examples while avoiding the conservative behavior that can result from remaining tied to those demonstrations.

The key role of the demonstrations is therefore to support exploration within an ongoing learning process. The authors report that HYPO significantly outperforms several baselines on challenging tasks involving sparse-reward MuJoCo, Google Research Football, and AirSim drone simulation. These empirical results support the usefulness of the guider-agent arrangement across the evaluated settings. The paper presents imperfect demonstrations as a practical starting point for learning, with policy updates helping the agent move beyond their limitations.
neurips-2023-hybrid-policy-optimization-.tldr: HYPO uses mutually updated guider and agent policies to turn a small set of imperfect demonstrations into more effective online exploration.

paragraphs: Models often perform poorly when deployment data differ from their training data. With multiple training environments, one strategy is to learn features that remain useful across environments. This paper pursues that goal using a nonparametric Nadaraya-Watson prediction head, which compares learned representations against a support set of labeled examples.

The main design choice concerns which examples enter that support set. The authors show that manipulating its composition can encode different causal assumptions. In particular, restricting it to one environment encourages the model to learn features that do not depend on the environment. Support-set construction thus becomes a way to shape representation learning.

The paper provides a causally motivated formulation of this modeling and training strategy and validates it on three challenging real-world computer vision tasks involving domain generalization. The approach matters because it places part of the invariance objective in the examples used to make predictions. The stated effect is encouragement toward invariant features, with empirical validation on the selected tasks, rather than a guarantee of successful transfer to every unseen distribution.
neurips-2023-learning-invariant-represen.tldr: Controlling a Nadaraya-Watson head's labeled support set encodes causal assumptions and can encourage representations that remain invariant across environments.

paragraphs: Standard autoregressive language training predicts tokens from left to right, even though the complete sequence is available during training. Meet in the Middle uses that availability by training in both directions. It encourages the left-to-right and right-to-left models to agree on their predicted token distributions at each position.

The primary goal is to improve the left-to-right language model through this bidirectional training arrangement. The paper describes improved data efficiency, using both directions to extract more learning value from the available sequences. Agreement between the directional models provides the connection between their otherwise differently ordered prediction tasks.

The two trained directions also support infilling, where a model completes a missing portion of a sequence. The proposed procedure builds that completion simultaneously from both sides. Experiments on programming languages and natural languages show significant improvements over existing pretraining approaches for both left-to-right generation and infilling. The contribution is a shared training principle that improves ordinary directional generation while also supplying components for a completion procedure that uses both boundaries of a gap.
neurips-2023-meet-in-the-middle-a-new-pr.tldr: Meet in the Middle trains language models in both directions with distribution agreement, improving generation and enabling completion from both sides of a gap.

paragraphs: When training data come from heterogeneous sources, the best mixture can depend on the target distribution. This paper tackles two connected costs: choosing source mixture weights for a target and repeatedly fitting a model when there are many targets. It seeks target-aware learning without repeating all of the work.

For mixture estimation, the authors formulate a convex-nonconcave compositional minimax problem and propose a stochastic algorithm with stationarity guarantees. These guarantees concern reaching a stationary solution, rather than establishing global optimality. For model fitting, they identify a regime in which target-optimal parameters can be represented as a nonlinear function of mixture coefficients.

In the offline setting, the paper proves that an overparameterized neural network trained by gradient descent can learn this function. This offers a way to predict model parameters instead of separately minimizing empirical risk for every target in that regime. The authors also give a label-efficient online algorithm for arbitrary sequences of mixture coefficients, with optimal regret. The results connect source selection with reusing the relationship between source mixtures and suitable models.
neurips-2023-mixture-weight-estimation-a.tldr: The paper provides guarantees for target-aware source weighting and, in a specified regime, predicting model parameters from mixture coefficients instead of retraining for every target.

paragraphs: Separating individual nuclei in three-dimensional images is important for biological research, but evaluating these algorithms requires extensive annotations. Earlier benchmarks either focused on two-dimensional images or labeled only a small number of three-dimensional cells. NIS3D addresses this gap with a large-volume, densely populated, completely annotated benchmark.

The dataset contains more than 22,000 cells from multiple commonly studied species. The authors developed semi-automatic annotation software to help construct it. Each cell receives labels from three independent annotators, enabling measurement of annotation variability. A confidence score for each cell supports comparisons that account for differences in annotation certainty.

Alongside a review of methods for segmenting dense three-dimensional nuclei, the authors evaluate selected state-of-the-art algorithms on NIS3D. Even the best evaluated methods remain far from human-level accuracy. The results also expose different methods' strengths and weaknesses, suggesting directions for further development. The benchmark's value comes from combining complete annotation with information about annotation variability, providing a more informative basis for assessing progress on a difficult segmentation task.
neurips-2023-nis3d-a-completely-annotate.tldr: NIS3D provides complete annotations for more than 22,000 cells and reveals a substantial gap between evaluated 3D nuclei segmentation methods and human accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper separates signals that have been superimposed using diffusion-based generative models. The method relies on statistical priors trained separately for independent sources. It combines these priors in an objective guided by maximum a posteriori estimation with an alpha-posterior, evaluated across several levels of Gaussian smoothing.

The motivating application is radio-frequency communication, where recovering the underlying encoded bits matters alongside separating the signals. The authors therefore evaluate bit error rate, which directly reflects errors in those recovered bits. Experiments on radio-frequency mixtures report a 95 percent reduction in bit error rate compared with classical and existing learning-based methods.

The theoretical analysis shows that the method's solutions asymptotically approach modes of an underlying discrete distribution. This connects the optimization procedure to the discrete structure of the sources of interest. The authors also interpret the approach as a multi-source extension of score distillation sampling. Together, the analysis and experiments link separately learned generative priors to signal recovery, with the reported performance improvement applying to the evaluated radio-frequency mixtures.
neurips-2023-score-based-source-separati.tldr: A diffusion-prior method separates independent signal sources and reports a 95 percent bit-error-rate reduction in radio-frequency mixture experiments.

paragraphs: SheetCopilot is an agent that translates natural-language requests into spreadsheet operations. It targets repetitive tasks that users may find burdensome or error-prone but lack the programming skills to automate. The central problem is turning a request into a sequence of software actions that actually fulfills the user's requirements.

The authors define atomic actions that abstract spreadsheet functionality and build a state-machine-based planning framework around them. This gives the language model a structured way to plan and interact with the spreadsheet. The contribution includes both this action interface and the planning arrangement used to control the software.

To evaluate the system, the paper introduces a dataset of 221 spreadsheet-control tasks and a fully automated evaluation pipeline. SheetCopilot correctly completes 44.3 percent of tasks with a single generation, substantially outperforming a strong code-generation baseline. This demonstrates an empirical advantage for the proposed control framework while also showing that many benchmark tasks remain unsolved in that setting. The benchmark makes successful task completion the basis for assessing language-model-driven spreadsheet automation.
neurips-2023-sheetcopilot-bringing-softw.tldr: SheetCopilot combines atomic spreadsheet actions with structured planning, completing 44.3 percent of 221 benchmark tasks in a single generation.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation is used as a building block in both generative and discriminative machine learning. This paper focuses on estimating density ratios, where the quantity of interest compares densities. Its concern is bias in the standard kernel estimates used for that task and how weighting can reduce it.

The authors use multidimensional calculus of variations to derive an optimal weight function. The weighting is designed to reduce bias in kernel-based density-ratio estimation. This treats the choice of weights as a mathematical optimization problem, producing a principled correction to the estimation procedure rather than simply accepting the bias of the standard estimates.

The stated benefits extend to estimates of prediction posteriors and information-theoretic measures, both of which the paper connects to density-ratio estimation. The work also examines fundamental aspects of density estimation from the perspective of algorithms built around kernel estimates. Its significance lies in improving a statistical component that other methods depend on: reducing bias at that component can improve the downstream quantities identified in the paper.
neurips-2023-variational-weighting-for-k.tldr: The paper derives an optimal weighting function that reduces bias in kernel density-ratio estimates and improves related posterior and information-theoretic estimates.

paragraphs: Uncertainty methods can flag suspicious examples without making clear what kinds of difficulty those examples represent. This paper proposes a framework for interpreting the examples an uncertainty method selects. The goal is to understand differences between methods through the nature of their warnings, beyond the fact that they produce warnings.

The central tool is a confusion density matrix, a kernel-based approximation of misclassification density. The framework uses it to organize flagged examples into three categories: out-of-distribution inputs, boundary examples, and inputs in regions with high in-distribution misclassification. These categories distinguish different situations that can all appear under the broad label of uncertainty.

Extensive experiments show that this categorization offers a distinct perspective for comparing uncertainty quantification methods. Two methods can be assessed according to which types of suspicious examples they identify, making their differences more interpretable. The contribution is an assessment framework and benchmark for understanding what uncertainty methods flag. It adds structure to the evaluation of their outputs rather than treating all flagged examples as a single undifferentiated group.
neurips-2023-what-is-flagged-in-uncertai.tldr: A confusion density matrix categorizes uncertainty warnings into out-of-distribution, boundary, and high-error in-distribution examples to clarify differences between methods.
